idiom_name: block-taking method with yield and ensure (the shape File.open uses internally)
implementation_notes: Ruby blocks are the body-as-argument form built into the language: the wrapper yields the resource and an ensure clause closes it, which is exactly Beck's During:/While: shape - File.open is the canonical example and closes the file through rb_ensure even when the block raises. What replaces the classic structure is `def open_during; setup; yield resource; ensure; teardown; end` plus the convention that every resource-taking core API has a block form (File.open, IO.popen, Dir.mktmpdir, Tempfile.create). Write the method when a protocol repeats or must centralize policy, and prefer the block form of the existing API over hand-rolled begin/ensure. A value result needs no extra work: the method returns the block's value.
code_sketch:
def open_during(path)
  file = File.open(path)              # setup
  yield file                          # body runs with the resource
  file
ensure                                # also runs on raise, return and break
  file&.close unless file.nil? || file.closed?
end

open_during("data.txt") { |f| process(f) }
pitfalls: ensure guarantees the teardown, but a return inside the block returns from the enclosing method (a non-local return) and a break returns from the yielding method: code after the call can be skipped in ways the reader does not see.

File.open without a block leaves the descriptor to the garbage collector - RuboCop's Style/FileOpen flags it - so the block form should be the default for anything but a resource whose lifetime the caller owns.
An exception raised inside ensure replaces the body's exception, so teardown must be written defensively (close only if not already closed, never raise on a successful path).
The block's arity is part of the contract: yielding a resource the block ignores, or using yield without a block, raises LocalJumpError; state whether the method requires a block.
